steps: Agree a form inventory with your team: each form's fields, which ones are required, and the spreadsheet its submissions land in.
Define each form in Google Sheets or Excel, and set up the Forms Submission Service so every submission lands in your chosen spreadsheet.
Publish each form, rendered on its Edge Delivery page by the Adaptive Forms Block, then submit test entries and check each one lands in the spreadsheet.
deliverables: Published forms on your Edge Delivery pages
Forms Submission Service set up for each form
Form inventory and test results
asks: The spreadsheet each form should write to, and who on your team may open it
The fields and wording for each form, approved by the form owner
risk: Personal data reaching a widely shared sheet: we agree who can open each spreadsheet and collect only the fields you approve.
outcome: Your simple forms run on your Edge Delivery pages, and every submission is stored in the spreadsheet you chose.

steps: Agree the LaunchPoint custom service with your Marketo administrator, and receive its Client ID and Client Secret, with the REST Identity URL, through a secure channel.
Create the Marketo Engage cloud configuration in AEM with those credentials and the REST Identity URL, so your forms can use the Marketo data model.
Test the connection to your Marketo Engage instance, and record the configuration and who owns the LaunchPoint credentials in a setup note.
deliverables: Marketo Engage cloud configuration in AEM
Connection test results
Setup note with credential ownership
asks: A Marketo Engage administrator who can create the LaunchPoint custom service and share its credentials
A named owner on your team for the LaunchPoint credentials after handover
risk: Credentials shared in the open or tied to one person: we receive them through a secure channel and record an owner on your team.
outcome: Your AEM instance is connected to your Marketo Engage instance, so your forms can be built on the Marketo data model and submit to Marketo.

steps: Agree each form's fields with your marketing operations team and map them to Marketo Engage fields in a mapping sheet, with consent wording and validation.
Build new forms on the Marketo Engage data model in the form wizard, or bind your existing forms to it, field by field from the mapping sheet.
Set the Submit to Marketo Engage action on each form, so every submission is sent to Marketo Engage for processing.
Submit test entries on each form and check that each one reaches the People database in Marketo Engage with every mapped field correct.
deliverables: Forms bound to the Marketo Engage data model
Field mapping sheet
Submission test results
asks: A marketing operations contact who knows your Marketo Engage fields and can approve the mapping
Approved consent wording and validation rules for each form
risk: A form field mapped to the wrong Marketo field, which fills the People database with bad data: we test every mapped field before a form goes live.
outcome: Each submission on your adaptive forms reaches the People database in Marketo Engage, with its fields mapped as your team agreed.

steps: Agree the form fields and the identity field with your data team, and create or extend the XDM schema for form data in your Experience Platform.
Enable the schema for Profile with its identity field, then create the dataset, the streaming connection and the API credentials the AEP Connector uses.
Check the setup against the AEP Connector's prerequisites, and record the schema, dataset, streaming connection and credential owner in a setup sheet.
deliverables: Profile-enabled XDM schema for form data
Dataset, streaming connection and API credentials
Setup sheet for the AEP Connector
asks: A data team contact who can approve schema changes in your Experience Platform
The identity field that should link a form submission to a profile
risk: A schema change that clashes with your existing profile data: we agree the identity field and the new fields with your data team first.
outcome: Your Experience Platform is ready to take form submissions: a profile-enabled schema, a dataset and a streaming connection for the AEP Connector.

steps: Create the Experience Platform cloud configuration in AEM, so your form authors can build on the XDM schemas available in Adobe Experience Platform.
Build each agreed form on its profile-enabled XDM schema, with the fields, labels and validation your team approved in a form specification.
Set the Submit to Adobe Experience Platform action on each form, with the streaming URL and dataflow ID from your Experience Platform setup.
Submit test entries under known test identities, and check that each one reaches the dataset and updates the matching profile in Real-Time CDP.
deliverables: Experience Platform cloud configuration in AEM
Forms built on profile-enabled XDM schemas
Form specifications and submission test results
asks: Approval of each form's fields, labels and validation from the form owner
Test identities your data team is happy for us to use in Experience Platform
risk: Test submissions that create or change real customer profiles: we test with agreed test identities and check the profiles before any form goes live.
outcome: Each form submission streams to Experience Platform and updates the customer's profile, so Real-Time CDP can use it for personalization.

steps: Agree with your Workfront team which forms send to Workfront Fusion and what each submission should start, and record it in a scenario plan.
Build the Fusion scenario starting with the AEM Forms module and a webhook, and connect it with the AEM service credentials.
Add the technical account to the forms-users group in AEM, and set each form's submit action to invoke the scenario.
Submit test entries on each form, and check that each one reaches the scenario with every field the plan expects.
deliverables: Workfront Fusion scenario triggered by your forms
Forms set to submit to the scenario
Scenario plan and test results
asks: An AEM administrator who can issue the service credentials and add the technical account to forms-users
A Workfront Fusion user who will own the scenario after handover
risk: Submissions lost when the scenario's connection stops working: we record the credential owner and test a failed run with your team before go-live.
outcome: Your adaptive forms submit straight to a Workfront Fusion scenario, ready to act on each submission, for example by starting work in Workfront.

steps: Map each request type on your forms to the Workfront work it should start: a project, assigned tasks, a notification or a status update.
Agree with your Workfront team who is assigned, who is notified and which form fields carry into Workfront for each request type.
Extend the Workfront Fusion scenario so each submission starts the agreed work, with the routing for every request type in the map.
Test each request type end to end with your team, from form submission to the project, tasks or status change in Workfront, and record sign-off.
deliverables: Extended scenario that starts work in Workfront
Request type map
End-to-end test results and sign-off
asks: The list of your request types and what each one should start in Workfront
A Workfront contact who can approve assignees, notifications and the fields carried over
risk: Work assigned to the wrong team or person: we test every request type with your Workfront team and record their sign-off before the forms go live.
outcome: Each form submission starts the right work in Workfront without rekeying: a project, assigned tasks, a notification or a status update.

steps: Agree which remote AEM Assets environment your Sites authors draw approved assets from through Dynamic Media with OpenAPI, and which placements use them.
Set the asset delivery repository and IMS client variables in Cloud Manager, as environment variables for AEM as a Cloud Service.
Configure the Image v3 component and HTTPS, so your authors can place approved assets from the remote AEM Assets environment in the Page Editor.
Test with your authors that they can pick remote assets on a sample page, and check the images render once the page is published.
deliverables: Cloud Manager environment variables for asset delivery
Image v3 component configured for remote assets
Author test results on a sample page
asks: A Cloud Manager user on your team who can set environment variables
A few authors to test picking remote assets on a sample page
risk: Authors expecting remote assets in Content Fragments, which work on AEM 6.5, not AEM as a Cloud Service: we agree up front which placements use remote assets.
outcome: Your Sites authors place approved assets from your remote AEM Assets environment straight onto pages in the Page Editor.

steps: Inventory the image placements on your page templates in a placement sheet, agreeing the size, crop and format each one needs.
Set up image modifiers, the URL parameters that transform images on the fly, on the Image v3 and Teaser v2 components for each placement.
Add smart crops where your Dynamic Media edition includes them, and list any other components that would need custom work to use modifiers.
Check a sample of pages on desktop and mobile, comparing each image's delivered size and format with the placement sheet, and fix any mismatch.
deliverables: Image modifiers set up for Image v3 and Teaser v2
Smart crop settings, where your edition includes them
Placement sheet and page check results
asks: Design guidance on image sizes and crops for each page template
Your Dynamic Media edition, so we know whether smart crops are included
risk: Images in other components, which need custom work to use modifiers: we list them early, so you decide which ones are worth the extra work.
outcome: Each image placement on your pages gets the right size and format from the DAM, through image modifiers on the Image v3 and Teaser v2 components.

steps: Agree with your campaign and content teams which content your campaigns and journeys should reuse, and model channel-ready Content Fragments for it.
Allow the Content Fragment API in the Dispatcher, so Journey Optimizer can pull your published fragments into campaigns and journeys.
Create the ajo-enabled tag for each Journey Optimizer sandbox, with your org ID and the sandbox name, and tag the agreed fragments.
Publish the tagged fragments, then check with your campaign team that they appear and render in a test campaign and a test journey.
deliverables: Channel-ready Content Fragments for campaigns and journeys
Dispatcher rule for the Content Fragment API
ajo-enabled tag for each sandbox
Test campaign and journey results
asks: The Journey Optimizer sandboxes that should draw on AEM content
A campaign team member to test fragments in a campaign and a journey
risk: Fragments missing from Journey Optimizer because a tag or publish step was skipped: we test every sandbox with a test campaign and journey before handover.
outcome: Your campaigns and journeys draw on approved Content Fragments from AEM Sites, tagged for each sandbox and published for your teams to use.

steps: Agree with your campaign team which fragment text should be personalized, and which profile or contextual attribute fills each placeholder.
Add the placeholders to the fragment text, and declare every placeholder as a parameter so Journey Optimizer can personalize it in real time.
Map each placeholder to its profile or contextual attribute in Journey Optimizer, and set up fragment variations for the agreed audiences or channels.
Test each variation against sample profiles, including one with an empty attribute, and agree with your team how that text should read.
deliverables: Personalized fragments with declared placeholders
Placeholder and attribute mapping sheet
Fragment variations for agreed audiences or channels
Variation test results
asks: The profile and contextual attributes your campaigns may use for personalization
Approval of the personalized wording and of each variation
risk: A placeholder that renders blank or wrong for some customers: we test every variation against sample profiles, empty attributes included, before use.
outcome: Your Content Fragments carry personalized text and variations, filled from profile or contextual attributes in Journey Optimizer for each audience or channel.

steps: Enable the AJO External References extension in AEM, so authors see which campaigns, journeys and templates use each Content Fragment.
Check that references come back from every organization and sandbox associated with your predefined tags, using fragments already in live campaigns.
Agree a check-before-you-change rule with your authors, train them to preview affected campaigns and journeys, and add it to your authoring guide.
deliverables: AJO External References extension enabled in AEM
Reference check on live fragments
Author guidance and a short training session
asks: The authors who edit fragments used in Journey Optimizer, for a short session
A few live campaigns or journeys that use AEM fragments, for testing
risk: An author changing a fragment a live campaign depends on: we train authors to preview every campaign, journey and template using it before they edit.
outcome: Your authors see and preview the campaigns, journeys and templates that use a fragment before they change it.

steps: Agree the source with your team: the existing pages index, once we check it holds only public content, or a site crawl with exclusions and a refresh schedule.
Set up the Content AI source on your AEM as a Cloud Service environment in Cloud Manager, and confirm it is Available with test searches.
Build the AEM Sites knowledge source in Composer by selecting the Content AI index, and attach Content AI Search to the Site Advisory skill.
Test the concierge against a golden set of real customer questions your pages answer, and review the answers with your reviewers.
deliverables: Content AI source, Available in Cloud Manager
AEM Sites knowledge source in Composer
Content AI Search on the Site Advisory skill
Golden-set test results
asks: A decision on the existing pages index or a site crawl, and any sections to exclude
Reviewers who know your site's content to judge the test answers
Cloud Manager access for your AEM as a Cloud Service environment
risk: Private or draft content reaching the concierge's answers: we check the index holds only public content, or set crawl exclusions, before connecting it.
outcome: Brand Concierge answers visitors from your AEM Sites pages through a Content AI index, with Content AI Search on the Site Advisory skill.

steps: Check with your web team that the AEM managed CDN is the site's outer CDN, since your own CDN in front would need its own routing.
Enable Brand Visibility's routing for AI agents in the Brand Visibility UI, so agentic traffic goes to the Edge Optimize backend service.
Test with the user agents of ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude that requests return the x-edgeoptimize-request-id header, and that visitors and search bots still get AEM's pages.
deliverables: Routing for AI agents enabled in the Brand Visibility UI
Test record for agent, visitor and search bot requests
asks: Someone on your web team who knows your CDN setup
Access to the Brand Visibility UI for your site
risk: Visitors or search bots served the wrong version of a page: we test each kind of request before and after the routing is switched on.
outcome: The AI agents Adobe supports get the optimized version of your pages where a fix is deployed, while visitors and search bots still get AEM's pages.

steps: Allow the AdobeEdgeOptimize/1.0 user agent in your site's robots.txt and in the traffic filter rules, through your normal release process.
Check that pages leave Dispatcher and the CDN with a Last-Modified header, sampling each type of page, and fix the configuration where it is missing.
Retest a sample of pages after the release and record the results, so no content fix is skipped because the header is missing.
deliverables: robots.txt and traffic filter rules allowing AdobeEdgeOptimize/1.0
Last-Modified header on pages from Dispatcher and the CDN
Page sample test results
asks: A developer who can change robots.txt, traffic filter rules and the Dispatcher configuration
A slot in your release schedule for the changes
risk: Content fixes skipped because pages lack a Last-Modified header: we check a sample of every page type before and after the release.
outcome: Your AEM site lets the AdobeEdgeOptimize/1.0 user agent in, and its pages carry a Last-Modified header, so content fixes are not skipped.

steps: Agree the page data to collect with your analytics team, starting with page name, site section and host, and record it in a measurement plan.
Connect the Tags property to AEM through its IMS and cloud configurations, and build data elements from the AEM Core Components data layer.
Add a Tags rule on the Adobe Client Data Layer's cmp:show event that sends each page view with Web SDK to Platform Edge Network.
Check that page views reach the Experience Platform dataset with every agreed field, then add the dataset to your CJA connection and data view.
deliverables: Tags property connected to AEM
Data elements and page view rule
Page views in the dataset and CJA data view
Measurement plan
asks: An analytics contact to agree the page data and the CJA data view
Access to your Tags property and the AEM cloud configurations
risk: Page names that do not match how your team reports: we agree the names and sections in the measurement plan before building the data elements.
outcome: Every page view on your AEM site reaches CJA with its page name, site section and host, ready for your analysts to report on.

steps: Agree with your analytics team which buttons and teaser CTAs to track, and how each CTA's ID and name should read in reports.
Add a Tags rule on the data layer's click event for those buttons and teaser CTAs, sending the CTA ID and name with Web SDK.
Click through a test set of CTAs, check each click arrives in the Experience Platform dataset, then add the CTA fields to your CJA data view.
deliverables: Tags rule for button and teaser CTA clicks
CTA clicks in the dataset and CJA data view
CTA test set and results
asks: The buttons and teaser CTAs your team wants to measure, by page or section
An analytics contact to approve the CTA names used in reports
risk: Clicks that arrive without a usable CTA name: we test a set of CTAs from each page template before the fields reach your data view.
outcome: Clicks on your site's buttons and teaser CTAs reach CJA with each CTA's ID and name, beside your page views.

steps: Inventory your custom components with your analytics team, and agree which author fields each view and click event should carry.
Extend each custom component's data layer model with those fields, and add dialog options so your authors can enter them.
Update the Tags and Web SDK mappings, and the CJA data view, so the agreed view and click events include the new fields.
Test each extended component on a sample page, from the author's entry to the field in the dataset and data view.
deliverables: Extended data layer models for your custom components
Author dialog fields for the data layer
Updated Tags, Web SDK and data view mappings
Component test results
asks: The list of custom components and the fields your analysts need from each
A content author to try the new dialog fields
risk: Authors leaving the new fields empty, so reports have gaps: we keep the fields few and clearly labeled, and check a sample of pages for empty fields before handover.
outcome: Views and clicks on your custom components reach CJA with the extra fields your authors enter, beside the Core Components data.

steps: Choose an approved reference page for each page type with your content team, and tidy each one, since Coworker uses it as the template for the layout.
Write a marketing brief template with goals, audience and keywords, so every request to Coworker carries the same guidance.
Pilot Coworker drafting a few real pages from a natural language prompt and a brief, with drafts opening in the Page Editor or Universal Editor.
Review each pilot draft with your editors against the brief and your style guide, and record what to change in the reference pages or brief.
deliverables: Approved reference page for each page type
Marketing brief template
Pilot drafts and review notes
asks: A content lead who can approve the reference page for each page type
A few real page requests from your team to use in the pilot
risk: Drafts that drift from your layout or voice: we tidy the reference pages first and review every pilot draft against the brief before wider use.
outcome: Your authors ask Coworker for a page draft from a brief, and it opens in the editor laid out like your approved reference page.

steps: Agree with your development lead which pipeline and environment actions may run through Coworker, and which need a second person's review.
Check that the developers who will use the AEM Cloud Manager Pipeline Troubleshooting skill have the Developer or Program Manager role in Cloud Manager.
Add Troubleshoot with AI and Dispatcher Insights to your release and support runbook, and walk your developers through a failed pipeline example.
deliverables: Agreed list of Coworker actions and review rules
Updated release and support runbook
Developer walkthrough session
asks: A development lead who can decide which actions need a second review
A Cloud Manager administrator to check developer roles
risk: A pipeline or environment change made through Coworker without a check: we write into the runbook which actions need a second person's review.
outcome: Your developers use Coworker for pipeline troubleshooting and Dispatcher work within agreed limits, written into the release and support runbook.

steps: Agree with your design team which approved Figma designs to import, and list the existing Content Fragment Models they might reuse.
Store the Figma access token in AEM, and import the agreed designs with Coworker to create Visual Content Fragments.
Review the Content Fragment Models, Content Fragments and HTML templates AEM creates, and reuse existing models where they fit instead of keeping duplicates.
Check each fragment against its Figma design with your designers, and record the import steps and naming rules for your team.
deliverables: Visual Content Fragments from approved Figma designs
Reviewed models and HTML templates
Import and naming guide
asks: The approved Figma designs to import, and a Figma access token
A designer to check each fragment against its design
risk: Duplicate Content Fragment Models that split your content: we review every model AEM creates and reuse existing ones where they fit.
outcome: Your approved Figma designs become Visual Content Fragments in AEM, built on reviewed models, with existing models reused where they fit.

steps: Agree the site structure and paths with your team, and whether stage and production are split into separate sites.
Create the site on AEM Author from the Edge Delivery Services with AEM authoring site template, and link your Edge Delivery code to it as the content source.
Give the publishing technical account its rights, set the path mapping, and add the separate production site where stage and production are split.
Edit and publish test pages in the Universal Editor, and check that each one appears on Edge Delivery at the expected path.
deliverables: AEM site created from the Edge Delivery template
Content source, rights and path mapping configured
Separate production site, where needed
Publishing test results
asks: Access to AEM Author and to your Edge Delivery code
A decision on whether stage and production run as separate sites
risk: Pages publishing to the wrong paths or site: we agree the path mapping first and test publishing before your authors start work.
outcome: Your authors manage pages in the Sites console, edit them in the Universal Editor and publish them from AEM to Edge Delivery.

steps: Inventory the blocks in your library, and agree with your authors which fields each block should let them edit.
Give each block its Universal Editor definition, model and filter, so authors can add and edit it in AEM with the agreed fields.
Keep the block code and styles in the Edge Delivery build, and test adding and editing each block in the Universal Editor on a sample page.
Publish the sample pages and check that every block renders on Edge Delivery as expected, then hand your authors a short block guide.
deliverables: Universal Editor definitions, models and filters for each block
Block inventory with agreed author fields
Published sample pages and test results
Author block guide
asks: Authors who can say which fields they need to edit in each block
Access to AEM and to your Edge Delivery code
risk: A block that edits well but breaks on the published page: we publish a sample page for every block before your authors build real pages.
outcome: Your authors add and edit every block in your library in the Universal Editor, and pages publish to Edge Delivery as designed.

steps: Agree the localized sites with your team: which MSM sites exist, the language or market each serves, and how Live Copy rollouts flow between them.
Turn on repoless for the project, then give each localized MSM site its own AEM configuration and Edge Delivery site on the shared code base.
Roll out a test change through Live Copy and check that each localized page publishes to its own site, not a neighbor's.
Record the steps for adding a new localized site in a short runbook, so your team can repeat them without a new code base.
deliverables: Repoless set up on the shared code base
AEM configuration and Edge Delivery site per localized site
Live Copy rollout test results
Runbook for adding a localized site
asks: The list of localized sites and the market or language each serves
An author who runs Live Copy rollouts today, to test with us
risk: A rollout publishing to the wrong localized site: we test a Live Copy rollout for every site before your authors use the new setup.
outcome: Each localized site is delivered by Edge Delivery Services from one shared code base, and Live Copy rollouts publish to the right site.

steps: Agree with your team which paths move to Edge Delivery in each phase, and record them in a phase plan with a rollback for each.
Route each phase's paths to Edge Delivery with origin selector rules in the CDN configuration, deployed through the config pipeline.
Set up push invalidation for the Edge Delivery paths, and keep every other page on AEM Publish until its phase comes.
Test each phase in the stage environment, checking that moved paths come from Edge Delivery and the rest from AEM Publish, before the production change.
deliverables: Phase plan with paths and rollback steps
Origin selector rules in the CDN configuration
Push invalidation for the Edge Delivery paths
Stage test results for each phase
asks: A decision on which sections of the site move in each phase
A slot in your release calendar for each phase's CDN change
risk: Visitors hitting broken or mixed pages during a phase: we test every phase on stage and keep a rollback of the routing ready for production.
outcome: Your site moves to Edge Delivery in phases on one domain, with each moved path served by Edge Delivery and the rest by AEM Publish.

steps: Agree the asset folders each site publishes from with your team, and grant the publishing technical account access to the private ones.
Include the required DAM paths in the site mapping, and assign the site's cloud configuration to the folders used for independent asset publishing.
Configure renditions that adhere to the limits of Edge Delivery, assign the processing profile to the agreed folders, reprocess existing assets and test them on a published page.
deliverables: Asset folder access and site mapping
Edge Delivery renditions and processing profile
Reprocessed assets and a published test page
asks: The asset folders each site should publish from, including any private ones
A DAM administrator who can grant folder access and assign processing profiles
risk: Images and videos outside the limits of Edge Delivery: we configure renditions within those limits and reprocess existing assets before pages go live.
outcome: Your AEM-authored pages publish their DAM assets to Edge Delivery, private folders included, in renditions within its limits.

steps: Agree the identities with your data team, then send AEM page views from the Tags property with Web SDK to a profile-enabled dataset.
Check on a sample of test visits that page views build profiles under the right merge policy.
Build the first behavior-based audience with your marketing team, such as visitors to one section, and check that the test visitors qualify.
deliverables: AEM page views in a profile-enabled dataset
Profile and merge policy check results
First behavior-based audience
asks: The identities your data team wants AEM visits stored under
A marketer to define the first behavior-based audience with us
risk: Visits split across profiles or merged into the wrong one: we agree the identities and check sample profiles under the merge policy first.
outcome: Visits to your AEM site build customer profiles in Real-Time CDP, ready for audiences based on how people browse.

steps: Agree with your data team the namespace for the AEM user ID, and how it matches the IDs in your CRM or order data.
Extend your site login to store the AEM user ID in the browser's session storage, and make it available to Tags.
Send the user ID in Web SDK's identity map under your own namespace, with the page views of signed-in visitors.
Sign in with test accounts and check that each visit joins the matching CRM or order data in one profile.
deliverables: AEM user ID sent in the identity map
Namespace and ID matching record
Test sign-in results with joined profiles
asks: Test accounts on your site login, with matching CRM or order records
A data team contact to agree the namespace and ID matching
risk: A user ID that does not match your CRM or order IDs, so profiles stay apart: we agree the match first and test it with test accounts.
outcome: Signed-in visits to your AEM site join your CRM or order data in one profile, under your own namespace.

steps: Set the site's delivery type to AEM Cloud Service in Sites Optimizer, and agree with your team who approves fixes before they deploy.
Add an allow rule for the scanner to your CDN traffic filter rules in Cloud Manager, matching its User-Agent and IP address, and update any IP allow lists.
Deploy an approved pilot fix from Sites Optimizer into AEM author, and check that your authors can review and publish it.
Record the setup, the approval route and the pilot result in a short handover note for your web team.
deliverables: Delivery type set to AEM Cloud Service
Scanner allow rule in your traffic filter rules
Pilot fix reviewed and published by your authors
Handover note
asks: A Cloud Manager user who can change the traffic filter rules
The IP allow lists in place on your site, and who owns them
An author to review and publish the pilot fix
risk: The scanner blocked by a traffic filter rule or allow list: we add the allow rule first and check the scan runs before the pilot fix.
outcome: Sites Optimizer scans your AEM site and deploys approved fixes into AEM author, where your authors review and publish them.

steps: Agree with your development lead how code fixes arrive: pull requests on a bring-your-own Git repository on GitHub, or a branch on a Cloud Manager standard repository.
Configure pull-request delivery for Cloud Manager bring-your-own Git, or branch delivery for Cloud Manager standard repositories, for Sites Optimizer's code fixes.
Agree the developer review, testing and release steps for code fixes, such as those for Core Web Vitals, Security and Form Accessibility opportunities.
Run a first code fix through the whole route, from pull request or branch to release, and record the steps in your release runbook.
deliverables: Pull-request or branch delivery for code fixes
Agreed review, testing and release steps
First code fix released and runbook updated
asks: A development lead to agree the review, testing and release route
Access to your Cloud Manager repository, or your GitHub repository for bring-your-own Git
risk: A code fix released without a developer's review: we route every fix through a pull request or branch and your agreed review and testing steps.
outcome: Sites Optimizer's code fixes reach your developers as pull requests or branches, and go live only through your own review and release steps.

steps: Turn on Preflight where your authors work: in the Page Editor toolbar on a supported AEM version, or through the Universal Editor extension your system administrator enables.
Agree with your content lead whether the Auto-Suggest or Auto-Optimize profile fits your authors, and assign it.
Train your authors to run SEO and accessibility audits with Preflight before they publish, using pages from your own site.
deliverables: Preflight turned on where your authors work
Auto-Suggest or Auto-Optimize profile assigned
Author training session and quick guide
asks: A system administrator to enable the Universal Editor extension, if your authors use it
Time from your authors for a hands-on training session
risk: Authors skipping the audit when deadlines press: we make Preflight a step in your publishing checklist and show authors the checks on their own pages.
outcome: Your authors run SEO and accessibility audits with Preflight in the editor they already use, before they publish.

steps: Map your AEM Multi-Site Manager and Language Copy structure with your team, from source pages to each language variant.
Document for each supported opportunity type, such as Alt Text, whether a fix updates the source or a local page, and any inheritance break you intend.
Take the rules to your content owners for approval, then test fixes on the affected variants and check each lands where the rules say.
deliverables: Multi-site rules for each supported opportunity type
Approved rules record
Variant test results
asks: Content owners for each site or language who can approve the rules
A current view of your source sites and their language variants
risk: A fix applied at the wrong level, source or local page, or an inheritance break nobody intended: we agree and test the rule for each opportunity type first.
outcome: Sites Optimizer fixes land in the right place across your sites and language variants, by rules your content owners approved.

steps: Set up the Developer Console project and the IMS, Target and legacy Target configurations in AEM, then configure the Link Externalizer.
Set the export format, HTML or JSON, and the Target workspace and domain on each Experience Fragment folder, as agreed with your Target team.
Agree the routine for lean Web variations with your authors: publish the fragment, export it to Target, and update the offer when the fragment changes.
Export a test fragment, use it as an offer in a test Target activity, and check it renders on the AEM page.
deliverables: IMS, Target and legacy Target configurations in AEM
Fragment folders set for export to Target
Publish, export and update routine for authors
Test activity results
asks: A Target administrator to agree the workspace and domain for exported fragments
The Experience Fragments your team wants to test or personalize first
risk: Offers in Target falling out of step with the fragments in AEM: we set up a publish, export and update routine and walk your authors through it.
outcome: Your Experience Fragments become offers in Target activities, so your team can test and personalize AEM pages with content your authors built.

steps: Agree with your app team which Content Fragments the headless app should use as offers, and in which Form-based activities.
Apply the Target configuration to the Content Fragment folders, and give the integration the Editor role in the Admin Console.
Export the agreed fragments to Target as JSON offers, and set them up in Form-based activities with your Target team.
Check with your app developers that the app renders each offer through Web SDK in a test activity before launch.
deliverables: Target configuration on the Content Fragment folders
Content Fragments exported as JSON offers
